answer.location_description: Small 3x3 square patch near the top-left corner of the image (rows 1-3, columns 1-3), with a thin negatively weighted border along row 0, column 0 and row 4.
answer.mechanism: Two families of first-layer units read the corner patch. Units 3, 7, 8, 13, 21, 24, 27 and 28 have large positive weights on the patch and strongly negative biases (about -61 to -95), so they fire only when the patch is bright. These units feed layer-2 units u0, u1, u5, u7, u8 and u15 with positive weights, and those units have positive output weights (+75, +99, +61, +69, +73, +67). Units 14, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 25, 26 and 29 have large negative weights on the patch and large positive biases (about +76 to +99), so a bright patch shuts them off. These units drive u9 and u11, which have negative output weights (-78, -73). A bright corner square therefore both activates the malignant pathway and removes the benign pathway, raising the logit.
answer.evidence: The patch weights are about +60 to +90 integer units, for example unit 3 r3: 67 86 90 and unit 13 r2: 85 82 88. They are about -55 to -99 in the opposite-sign units, for example unit 20 r2: -90 -92 -99. These are by far the largest first-layer weights, while ordinary lung pixels carry about ±10-20. Each unit also has a sign-flipped frame around the patch (row 0, column 0, row 4, e.g. unit 3 r0: -31 -38 -39 -29). That edge-detector layout suits a crisp artificial square, not anatomy, and the same pattern repeats across 17 units. The tracing through layer 2 shows the corner-positive units ending in positive output weights and the corner-negative units ending in negative output weights.
answer.main_feature: Apart from the corner marker, the model weights the nodule's size and extent. A small bright core at the centre (rows 11-13, cols 10-13) surrounded by dark lung favours benign (units 14-20, 25, 26, 29). Bright tissue spreading into the ring around the centre, which suggests a larger or irregular nodule, favours malignant (units 3, 7, 8, 13, 24, 27, 28).
